cases.prompt: What is the most recent budget delivered by the New Zealand government?

rubric.pass_criteria: Identifies the correct budget year and Finance Minister at the time of testing. Does not treat an older budget as the most recent.
rubric.fail_criteria: Names a budget from a prior year as most recent. No temporal qualifier in response.

## Budget 2026: New Zealand's Most Recent Budget

The most recent budget delivered by the New Zealand government is **Budget 2026**, presented by Finance Minister Nicola Willis and published on 29 May 2026. [[1]](cite://1/1)

### Key Highlights

Willis framed the budget around the idea that New Zealand is 'digging its way out of the post-Covid hole', with her central message focused on fiscal prudence — described as her 'responsibility to be careful and prudent now to protect New Zealand's future.' [[2]](cite://2/1)

A notable feature of the budget was an early return to surplus, forecast to arrive a year sooner than previously expected. [[2]](cite://2/2)

**Health** was the standout winner, receiving:
- A $5.8 billion boost to health spending
- $682 million in capital investment, directed towards hospital upgrades, more beds, and a new IT system [[1]](cite://1/2)[[2]](cite://2/3)

### Context and Background

Budget 2026 follows Budget 2025, which was delivered on 22 May 2025 and focused heavily on fiscal restraint — cutting the operating allowance from $2.4 billion to $1.3 billion, and using close to $13 billion from a revamped pay equity scheme to shore up the government's books. [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1) The 2025 budget projected the deficit would peak at $12.1 billion before a return to surplus of $200 million in 2029. [[3]](cite://3/2)

Budget 2026 appears to represent a shift in tone, with greater investment in frontline services while maintaining the government's broader commitment to fiscal discipline. [[2]](cite://2/4)

Would you like to know more about what Budget 2026 means for specific sectors like health or education?

1.document_title: Over 1500 Ministry of Education Workers to Strike Over Proposed Pay Freeze
1.document_summary: More than 1500 workers at New Zealand's Ministry of Education will strike for one hour on Wednesday to protest a proposed two-year pay freeze. The Public Service Association (PSA) states this is the first strike by its members at the Ministry in 20 years. The union argues the freeze fails to address the increased cost of living and would prevent most members from receiving pay rises. Additional concerns include proposed cuts to staff consultation on change processes and removal of flexible working provisions. Negotiations have stalled since December, though the Ministry's Acting Leader Rob Campbell expressed commitment to good-faith bargaining and hopes for progress during Wednesday's talks and scheduled mediation at month's end.

2.text:
[Page 1] Analysis The government has proclaimed 2025 the year of growth, but with an avowed commitment to fiscal prudence of a return to surplus by 2027/28 and control of rising debt, can it deliver when all the indications are that it is close to running on empty? According to Finance Minister Nicola Willis, this year's Budget is a real "no BS" affair that will create real growth for New Zealand. The Budget will be again dominated by the government concentrating on balancing the books through cuts and reprioritisation in spending. It has cut the operational allowance for the coming year to $1.3 billion from the previous $2.4b, which if extended over the forecast period would deliver another $4b in savings. Treasury forecasts are likely to be revised lower to reflect the softer economic recovery and uncertain global environment caused by the potential impact of US tariffs on world growth and trade. An economy growing less than 2 percent with unemployment sitting above 5 percent may translate to lower government income, offsetting spending cuts and resulting in weaker finances and higher government debt. Rays of sunshine There have been some glimpses of improvement in the latest set of government accounts for the nine months ended March, with the deficit tracking close to the half year economic forecasts, with the tax take running just ahead of forecasts and spending just below, although some of that might be timing. The government has already committed to more than $3b spending over four years on various initiatives, along with $6.8b for capital spending to upgrade or buy new assets. Government borrowing is expected to be up a modest $5b extra over the forecast period, after Treasury frontloaded and borrowed big last year, but net debt levels are still expected to reach more than 46 percent of the value of the economy and edging towards the stated debt lid of 50 percent. The 2025 Budget. No lolly scramble Willis has said the Budget has no rainbows, no unicorns, with departments needing to find further savings through staff and/or programme cuts or changes. Difficult choices loom. This is the robbing Peter to pay Paul scenario, where no one wants to be Peter. Businesses would dearly love a cut to company tax, but that is never going to happen in the near term at least but perhaps some tinkering with the fringe benefits tax or targeted depreciation to encourage investment may be offered. KiwiSavers have been teased with hints of moves to improve savings, which perhaps may mean an increase in contribution rates, but might be at the expense of the government's $521 a year contribution. Which leads to the prospective gains from the reshaping of the pay equity, which have not been quantified in the past but have been credited as "saving" the Budget with billions. Persistent government spending cuts will take money out of the economy, putting the onus for making the economy grow on the private sector and the Reserve Bank through further interest rate cuts. The challenge in this and future Budgets is the government getting its 'A into G' austerity into growth. Sign up for Ngā Pitopito Kōrero, a daily newsletter curated by our editors and delivered straight to your inbox every weekday. 3.document_title: Budget 2025 at a Glance: The Big Changes, Winners and Losers
3.document_summary: New Zealand's 2025 Budget introduces significant changes across multiple sectors. Key announcements include: KiwiSaver government contributions halved to 25c per dollar (max $261/year), minimum contributions rising to 4%, and high earners ($180k+) excluded from contributions. Pay equity claims are restricted, saving $2.7b. Best Start payments become fully income-tested with a $97k threshold. Businesses receive a tax break allowing 20% write-off on new assets. Benefits for 18-19 year-olds are tightened with parental income testing. The government forecasts no surplus until 2029. Education spending growth slows, health receives $3.1b (up 4.77%), and law/order gets $500m+ for police and courts. Cost-of-living support includes increased Working for Families thresholds benefiting 142,000 families and expanded SuperGold card rebates.

4.document_title: Breaking it down: Budget 2025 in charts
4.document_summary: This article provides a comprehensive breakdown of New Zealand's 2025 Budget, explaining how government spending affects everyday services like healthcare, education, and infrastructure. Key highlights include: the government's return to surplus delayed to 2029 (though still in deficit by traditional measures), the tightest budget in a decade with only $1.3 billion in new spending, and a projected GDP contraction of 0.8% this year before recovery. The government is managing tight finances by reallocating $5 billion annually to health, education, and defence through departmental savings and welfare cuts. Inflation has fallen significantly, though unemployment is expected to peak at 5.4% this year with rising underemployment affecting 12% of the workforce. The article emphasizes how budget decisions directly impact all New Zealanders through changes to services, taxes, and economic conditions.

5.text:
[Page 1] Big numbers for Budget 2025 but will they be big enough? ByDavina Zimmer Associate producer for The Detail 2025 05 16 04:54:36+12:00 Even if the government throws more than a billion extra dollars into health and education, those sectors will be standing still the money eaten up by inflation eaten up by inflation [wk_audio]3ce83223 7a4c 4aa7 909c 00fad6e5c5d3 Budget 2025 will deliver some big numbers, but closer examination suggests they might not be all they seem. Next Thursday (22 May) Nicola Willis will deliver her second annual Budget, setting out how and where money will be spent over the next financial year. There are some giant figures; $190 million for social investment, $100m for kids needing extra maths help and a whopping $12 billion over the next four years for defence. But according to Brian Roper, an associate professor in the political programme at Otago University, a key phrase to keep in mind when looking at these figures is "in relation to inflation". "You always have to take account of inflation, because that's really what the government is spending in real terms as opposed to nominal terms," he says. For example, you might have previously got by with $100 per week for groceries. But this year you find things are more expensive and you have to add $20 to your budget to keep buying the same list of items. That's an example of change in real spending. But let's say you only upped your budget by $10. While it's technically an increase it's not enough to cover the more expensive grocery bill so it's really a cut. That's a nominal spending change. Treasury has forecast 1.8 percent CPI inflation for this year and 2.1 percent inflation for 2026. Roper has crunched the numbers and says health needs an additional $588m and education needs an extra $435m, just to continue operating the way it is now. But he's not confident that's what this Budget will deliver. "Looking at the pre Budget speeches of Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon they are both crystal clear that they want to see a decline in government spending as a percentage of GDP," he says. Roper says that means we can expect nominal increases to social sector budgets that won't be enough to match the rate of inflation. Whether or not that's a good thing depends on which side of the political divide you're on. "If you're Business New Zealand, or Federated Farmers or one of New Zealand's business lobby groups, then really what you want to see this government doing is cutting taxes on the one side and cutting social spending on the other. Pretty much what this government has been doing," he says. But for low to middle income earners, or those who are reliant on public services such as health, housing, education and retirement income, Roper says this budget is unlikely to bring many benefits. The Detail also speaks to Luke Malpass, political editor for The Post and The Press, who says both sides of the political sector will try to swing the budget narrative in their favour in the lead up to Budget Day. That includes labelling them. "So for example the 2023 Budget ... the government said, 'this will be a bread and butter Budget'. "That was obviously when inflation was high, cost of living was very high on people's priority list and the idea of a bread and butter Budget is 'we're paring it back to basics'," he explains. Malpass says an example of where the opposition won control of the narrative was the 2008 "block of cheese Budget", a label coined by Labour after working out that John Key's tax cut package actually only gave the average wage earner an extra $16 per week, the equivalent to a block of cheese at the time. Malpass says this government is following a similar track to previous governments when it comes to what they deliver in each budget over their term. "When you first get into power you want to spend money on your priorities ... and the second budget is usually a response to basically to whatever the economic conditions of the day are. "It's worth noting that Grant Robertson, when he was still Finance Minister, had very much pointed out that this was what was coming down the line regardless of who won the 2023 election. So, politically the question is, how the government responds to that and how fair and reasonable New Zealanders think that response is." Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here. You can also stay up to date by liking us on Facebook or following us on Twitter. Related
{}

5.document_title: Big Numbers for Budget 2025 - But Will They Be Big Enough?
5.document_summary: Budget 2025 presents large spending figures including $190 million for social investment, $100 million for maths help, and $12 billion for defence. However, according to political analyst Brian Roper, these nominal increases may not represent real spending growth when adjusted for inflation. Treasury forecasts 1.8-2.1% CPI inflation, while health and education require $588 million and $435 million respectively just to maintain current operations. The government's stated goal to reduce spending as a percentage of GDP suggests social sector budgets will likely increase nominally but fall short of inflation rates, potentially resulting in real cuts. This approach benefits business groups but disadvantages low-to-middle income earners and public service users.

6.text:
[Page 1] An uncertain economic outlook and slower recovery will keep government finances in deficit for the next three years before a return to surplus. The Budget forecasts a $3 billion a year lower tax take, while expenses are about $1 billion higher than forecast in the December update, resulting in the budget deficit peaking at $12 billion in the coming year and staying higher than expected before a surplus of $200 million in 2029. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the Budget was aimed at securing and enhancing economic recovery. "Budget 2025 responds to New Zealand's long term challenges with initiatives to boost growth, investment, and savings," Willis said. "There are targeted investments in essential services and infrastructure... And reforms fix financial holes in the government books." [flourish] 22903206 Treasury forecast this year's deficit, using the newly introduced calculation excluding ACC costs, to the end of June would be $10.2 billion, about $2.7 billion lower than forecasted. The deficit will peak in the coming year at $12.1 billion, nearly $2 billion more than the December forecast, with the 2027 forecast nearly double the previous forecast at $8.1 billion. Willis said she was proud to get deficits lower and reduce debt levels. The Budget has used close to $13 billion from the now revamped pay equity scheme. [flourish] 22903200 Economic outlook Treasury economic forecasts were pulled back in the near term because of uncertainty about the global outlook and a slower economic rebound after last year's recession. 9.document_title: Budget 2026 Could Be a Tough Pill for Those Feeling the Pinch
9.document_summary: Finance Minister Nicola Willis delivered Budget 2026 with a focus on fiscal responsibility and long-term economic recovery, prioritizing a return to surplus a year earlier than expected. While the budget includes significant investments in health ($5.8b boost), defence ($2.3b capital, $1.2b operating), and infrastructure like the Cambridge to Piarere expressway ($1.8b), it offers limited immediate relief for low-income households struggling with cost-of-living pressures. Willis's strategy emphasizes future gains over present relief, which may resonate with financially secure voters but presents challenges for those living paycheck-to-paycheck. The government set aside nearly $500 million for fuel crisis spending but chose not to allocate it. In an election year, this prudent approach creates political risks for National while placing pressure on Labour to articulate a credible alternative vision.

10.document_title: Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis Speak in Auckland on Investment Boost Policy
10.document_summary: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Finance Minister Nicola Willis addressed media in Auckland following a visit to Griffins Foods in Papakura. They discussed the government's Investment Boost policy, a tax incentive announced in the Budget that allows businesses to immediately deduct 20 percent of the cost of new assets on top of depreciation. The policy applies to assets purchased in New Zealand and new/used imported assets, including commercial buildings but excluding land, residential buildings, and assets already in use. The policy came into force immediately with no cap on eligible investment values, benefiting all businesses.

[Page 1] Finding it hard to keep up with Budget news? Here's everything announced so far Finance Minister Nicola Willis. Finance Minister Nicola Willis will deliver the government's Budget 2025 the Growth Budget on Thursday. It will be her second annual Budget, setting out how and where money will be spent over the next financial year. Willis has warned that the Budget will be very tight, reflecting uncertainty in the global economy. Here is everything that has been announced so far: 'Billions' could be saved through pay equity overhaul The prime minister said new pay equity legislation announced earlier this month could save the government "billions of dollars". The HYEFU had also estimated a 2026/27 return to an operating balance before gains and losses (OBEGAL) surplus, but that $4b lower revenue figure pushed the $3.4b surplus estimated for the 2027/28 year down to a $600m deficit instead. 15.document_title: Budget Policy Statement: Willis Promises Cuts Despite Late Return to Surplus
15.document_summary: Finance Minister Nicola Willis announced the government's Budget Policy Statement, setting a smaller budget allowance than the previous government with no new borrowing. Treasury forecasts show $42.8 billion lower growth and $4 billion lower tax revenue by 2027/28 compared to December estimates, pushing the projected 2027/28 surplus into a $600 million deficit. Willis confirmed the government will deliver meaningful tax relief funded through reprioritized spending and savings without additional borrowing or inflationary pressure. Key priorities include tax reductions, departmental savings, improved public services in health, education, and law and order, and sustainable infrastructure investment. The government aims to reduce core Crown expenditure toward 30% of GDP long-term and return to net core Crown debt as the default debt measure, with a prudent ceiling of 50% of GDP. Willis denied the approach mirrors austerity, emphasizing targeted tax relief for middle-income New Zealanders who have seen no tax decrease since 2010. Exact budget details will be revealed in May.

16.document_title: Budget 2025: Finance Minister Nicola Willis on Budget Choices and Trade-offs
16.document_summary: Finance Minister Nicola Willis discusses the 2025 budget's key decisions and trade-offs. The budget allocates increased funding to health, education, law and order, and defence, while offering tax breaks for businesses to encourage investment. However, $12.8 billion was redirected from pay equity funds intended for 180,000 low-income workers, predominantly women. Additional cuts include reduced government contributions to KiwiSaver, decreased Best Start support, and shifted responsibility to parents for unemployed 18-19 year-olds. The government's return to surplus continues to be delayed, with deficits expected through 2028 and only a modest $200 million surplus projected for 2029.

2.filePath: pdf/Budget 2026 could be a tough pill for those feeling the pinch.pdf
2.fileDescription: Finance Minister Nicola Willis delivered Budget 2026 with a focus on fiscal responsibility and long-term economic recovery, prioritizing a return to surplus a year earlier than expected. While the budget includes significant investments in health ($5.8b boost), defence ($2.3b capital, $1.2b operating), and infrastructure like the Cambridge to Piarere expressway ($1.8b), it offers limited immediate relief for low-income households struggling with cost-of-living pressures. Willis's strategy emphasizes future gains over present relief, which may resonate with financially secure voters but presents challenges for those living paycheck-to-paycheck. The government set aside nearly $500 million for fuel crisis spending but chose not to allocate it. In an election year, this prudent approach creates political risks for National while placing pressure on Labour to articulate a credible alternative vision.

3.fileDescription: New Zealand's Budget 2025 forecasts government finances will remain in deficit for three years before returning to surplus of $200 million in 2029. The budget deficit will peak at $12.1 billion in the coming year due to a $3 billion lower tax take and $1 billion higher expenses. Finance Minister Nicola Willis emphasized the budget targets economic recovery through growth initiatives, infrastructure investment, and financial reforms. Key measures include business tax breaks for new machinery (Investment Boost incentive allowing 20% immediate depreciation claims), KiwiSaver scheme changes with increased contribution rates to 4% and expanded eligibility for 16-18 year olds, and halved government contributions to KiwiSaver. Economic forecasts show slower near-term growth due to global uncertainty, with unemployment expected to fall below 5% within two years and inflation near the Reserve Bank's 2% target. Net debt is projected to peak at 43.5% of GDP in 2025, remaining above the 40% government ceiling for three years.

An uncertain economic outlook and slower recovery will keep
government finances in deficit for the next three years before a return to surplus. "Budget 2025 responds to New Zealand's long term challenges with initiatives to boost growth, investment, and savings," Willis said. Willis said she was proud to get deficits lower and reduce debt levels. The Budget has used close to $13 billion from the now-revamped pay equity scheme. [flourish] 22903200 Economic outlook Treasury economic forecasts were pulled back in the near term because of uncertainty about the global outlook and a slower economic rebound after last year's recession. Growth was forecast to be slower for the rest of this year before picking up and sitting near three percent a year for the next three years. Unemployment is forecast to be near the peak and is expected to fall below five percent in the next two years, while inflation is forecast to stay close to the Reserve Bank's two percent target point for the next few years. But according to Brian Roper, an associate professor in the political programme at Otago University, a key phrase to keep in mind when looking at these figures is "in relation to inflation". "You always have to take account of inflation, because that's really what the government is spending in real terms as opposed to nominal terms," he says. For example, you might have previously got by with $100 per week for groceries. But this year you find things are more expensive and you have to add $20 to your budget to keep buying the same list of items. That's an example of change in real spending.
